introLesson.title: Introduction to Frankenstein

sections.authorBiography: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on 30 August 1797, the daughter of two of the most famous radical writers of the 1790s: the philosopher William Godwin (author of Political Justice) and the feminist Mary Wollstonecraft (author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman). Wollstonecraft died of puerperal fever about eleven days after the birth, so Mary grew up with her mother's books rather than her mother. In 1814, at sixteen, she left England with the married poet Percy Bysshe Shelley; they married in December 1816, weeks after his first wife's suicide. She began Frankenstein at eighteen and published it at twenty. Her adult life was marked by loss: three of her four children died young, and Percy drowned in Italy in July 1822. She supported herself and her surviving son by writing, produced novels including The Last Man (1826), edited Percy's poems, and died in London on 1 February 1851.
sections.historicalContext: The novel was born in the summer of 1816, the "year without a summer," when ash from the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia chilled and darkened Europe. Mary, Percy, her stepsister Claire Clairmont, Lord Byron and Byron's physician John Polidori were kept indoors near Lake Geneva, and Byron proposed that each write a ghost story. The science in the air was electricity and life: Luigi Galvani had made dissected frogs' legs twitch with current, and in 1803 his nephew Giovanni Aldini publicly applied current to the corpse of an executed man in London. The book also belongs to Romanticism, a movement that prized feeling, nature and the solitary genius, and that was fascinated by Prometheus, the Titan who stole fire for humankind and was punished for it; the novel's subtitle is The Modern Prometheus. Behind it, too, is Mary's inheritance from her parents' arguments about education, injustice and how society makes people what they are.

publicationAndReception.publication: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously in three volumes on 1 January 1818 (London: Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor and Jones), in an edition of about 500 copies, with a preface by Percy Shelley and a dedication to William Godwin. A second edition (1823), arranged by Godwin, named Mary as author after a stage version, Richard Brinsley Peake's Presumption, became a hit. In 1831 she revised the text heavily for Colburn and Bentley's Standard Novels and added the Introduction that tells the story of its origin; that 1831 text is the one we read.
publicationAndReception.then: Early reviews were split. Walter Scott, in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine (March 1818), praised its "original genius" and assumed Percy Shelley was the author; John Wilson Croker in the Quarterly Review called it "a tissue of horrible and disgusting absurdity." Many reviewers were uneasy with a story that seemed to question God and moral order, and with an anonymous author linked to Godwin's radicals.
publicationAndReception.now: Today Frankenstein is one of the most taught novels in English. Brian Aldiss (Billion Year Spree, 1973) called it the origin of science fiction; feminist critics beginning with Ellen Moers (Literary Women, 1976) read it as a "birth myth" shaped by Mary's experience of pregnancy and infant death; others read it through politics, race, disability and bioethics. Its title has become shorthand in debates about genetic engineering and artificial intelligence, and 2018 brought bicentenary editions and projects worldwide.

sections.overview: A ship's captain, Robert Walton, sailing toward the North Pole, writes letters to his sister. In the ice he rescues a dying stranger, Victor Frankenstein, who tells him how, as a young student, he discovered the secret of life and built a living being. What happens to Victor, his family and his creation is told in three nested voices: Walton's, Victor's and, at the center, the creature's own. The book asks what we owe the things we make and the people we reject.

mainThemes.note: what a maker owes what it makes; watch how often the creature asks to be cared for and how Victor answers.
the hunger to discover, shared by Walton and Victor; ask whether the book condemns curiosity or something more specific.
almost every character is cut off from someone; notice who is allowed to belong and why.
is anyone born a monster, or are monsters made by how they are treated?
mountains, ice and storms that awe and dwarf human beings.

sections.whyItMatters: Frankenstein is the founding story for every argument about technology that outruns responsibility, from gene editing to artificial intelligence, and its creature still speaks for anyone judged by appearance before being heard. It also shows students that a teenager wrote one of the most influential books in the world.

spoilerOverview.text: Victor abandons the creature the moment it wakes. Rejected by every human it meets, the creature kills Victor's brother William (and frames Justine, who is executed), demands a mate, and, when Victor destroys the half-made female, kills Clerval and then Elizabeth on her wedding night. Victor pursues the creature to the Arctic and dies on Walton's ship; the creature mourns him and vanishes into the dark to die.

passage.quote: I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together
passage.use: Shelley's 1831 account of the waking vision that became the novel. Note "unhallowed" (unholy) and "thing": before we have read a page, the creator is a student and the creation is not yet a person.

flags: The exact night of the ghost-story proposal and of Mary's waking dream is uncertain: her 1831 account compresses events, and Polidori's diary points to mid-June 1816. Present the 1831 story as her own later recollection.
The extent of Percy Shelley's edits to the 1818 manuscript is debated (Charles E. Robinson's 2008 edition marks his contributions). He wrote the 1818 Preface; the novel is Mary's.
The first-edition print run is usually given as about 500 copies; treat it as approximate.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “I saw the pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together” slowly and put it in my own words: In her 1831 introduction, Shelley describes seeing, eyes closed, a pale student of forbidden arts kneeling beside the thing he had assembled. Next, craft. I notice the creature is called only "the thing he had put together," a phrase that refuses it a name or a human status from the start. The strongest word is “unhallowed”: it means unholy, so the science is framed as a violation of something sacred. Then, effect. What does Shelley's waking vision tell us about the novel she will write? My answer: Shelley presents the novel's seed as a nightmare of a creator who has crossed a forbidden line; the image of maker and made, frightened and unnamed, is the relationship the whole novel examines.

segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): A ship's captain, Robert Walton, sailing toward the North Pole, writes letters to his sister. In the ice he rescues a dying stranger, Victor Frankenstein, who tells him how, as a young student, he discovered the secret of life and built a living being. What happens to Victor, his family and his creation is told in three nested voices: Walton's, Victor's and, at the center, the creature's own. The book asks what we owe the things we make and the people we reject. Themes to track: creation and responsibility: what a maker owes what it makes; watch how often the creature asks to be cared for and how Victor answers. ambition and knowledge: the hunger to discover, shared by Walton and Victor; ask whether the book condemns curiosity or something more specific. isolation and companionship: almost every character is cut off from someone; notice who is allowed to belong and why. nature and nurture: is anyone born a monster, or are monsters made by how they are treated? the sublime: mountains, ice and storms that awe and dwarf human beings.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Shelley began Frankenstein at eighteen, in the summer of 1816 at Lake Geneva, during a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron and Percy Shelley, at a time when scientists were experimenting with electricity on dead bodies. How might that setting and science shape the novel? Answer: Accept answers such as: galvanism made reanimation seem possible; the contest pushed her toward horror; she was surrounded by Romantic poets who prized nature and feeling; she had already lost a baby, which may connect to themes of creation and loss.

introLesson.objective: Students will explain, in a 3-sentence exit ticket, how one fact about Mary Shelley's life or times connects to the costs of unchecked ambition in “Frankenstein”, and will set up a reading journal with a prediction and a question for each of 3 themes (the costs of unchecked ambition, creation and responsibility, isolation and the need for companionship).

criticalVoices.quote: This is a novel, or more properly a romantic fiction, of a nature so peculiar, that we ought to describe the species before attempting any account of the individual production.
criticalVoices.speaker: Walter Scott (attrib.), novelist and critic
criticalVoices.source: "Remarks on Frankenstein, or the Modern Prometheus; A Novel," Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine 2:12 (March 1818), p. 613 (opening sentence)
criticalVoices.useNote: Bell-ringer: Scott could not name the genre in 1818. What would you call it (Gothic, science fiction, philosophical romance)? Defend one label with a detail from the Introduction.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Classify the novel's genre and explain how its structure (frame narrative, "marvellous" premise) shapes meaning.

lessonPlan.title: Frankenstein unit
lessonPlan.author: Mary Shelley
lessonPlan.editionNote: The reading text is Mary Shelley's revised 1831 edition (Standard Ebooks, from Project Gutenberg #42324), which also prints the 1818 Preface and the 1831 Introduction. In 1818 Elizabeth is Victor's cousin; in 1831 she is the orphaned daughter of a Milanese nobleman, adopted by Victor's mother. Chapter breaks also differ (e.g. around Chapter III). Cite this edition.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–12 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Frankenstein.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Frankenstein: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Frankenstein has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to the costs of unchecked ambition.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Frankenstein. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this chapter, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the chapter on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the chapter to the costs of unchecked ambition.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the chapter quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Frankenstein.

essentialQuestions: What does Frankenstein suggest about the costs of unchecked ambition?
What does Frankenstein suggest about creation and responsibility?
What does Frankenstein suggest about isolation and the need for companionship?
What does Frankenstein suggest about nature versus nurture?
What does Frankenstein suggest about the sublime power of nature?
objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the novel in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.

By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make. This develops creation and responsibility: Shelley calls the book her "hideous progeny" and sends it out into the world, as Victor does his creature; but unlike Victor she wishes it to "prosper." The author models the care the character fails to give.

By citing Dr. Darwin and German physiologists it claims the event is "not of impossible occurrence," and by naming domestic affection and virtue as its aims it answers the charge that a horror story is immoral. Isolation through allusion. The words “Like Adam, I was apparently united by no link to any other being in existence” (Chapter XV, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
Introduction

By citing Dr. Darwin and German physiologists it claims the event is "not of impossible occurrence," and by naming domestic affection and virtue as its aims it answers the charge that a horror story is immoral. The words “The event on which this fiction is founded, has been supposed, by Dr. Darwin, and some of the physiological writers of Germany, as not of…” (Preface, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: The Preface claims the story shows "the amiableness of domestic affection"; keep this phrase on the board. The novel will test it: domestic love is shown, then destroyed.

Allusion

An allusion that promises he will not offend against nature; readers who know Coleridge sense danger. The words “I shall kill no albatross” (Letter II, paragraph 6) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: the desire for a sympathetic friend is the thread connecting Walton, Victor and the creature.

The heart of Victor's ambition: more than anyone before. The words “more, far more, will I achieve” (Chapter III, paragraph 17) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: Waldman says modern scientists "penetrate into the recesses of nature"; Victor answers with a vow to go further.
Chapter V

The creature's first gesture is reaching; Victor's response is flight. Key evidence that the creature is abandoned before it acts. The words “one hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me, but I escaped” (Chapter V, paragraph 3) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: the moment of birth is the moment of abandonment.

Guilt imagined as hell. The words “I was seized by remorse and the sense of guilt, which hurried me away to a hell of intense tortures” (Chapter IX, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the sublime: nature offers temporary relief from guilt.

Human violence comes first. The words “some fled, some attacked me” (Chapter XI, paragraph 10) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops nature and nurture: he begins innocent; humans attack him on sight.

He remembers "considerable difficulty" in understanding his first sensations, a newborn's helplessness, and the villagers' response to his approach is that "some fled, some attacked me," so hostility comes from them. The words “It is with considerable difficulty that I remember the original era of my being” (Chapter XI, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: Victor feels "an insurmountable barrier" between himself and others.
Foreshadowing

He confesses only in riddles ("I am the assassin") and fixates on the creature's threat to himself, so the one person who loves him never learns the danger she is in. The words “I am the assassin of those most innocent victims; they died by my machinations” (Chapter XXII, paragraph 6) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: secrets poison his relationship with Elizabeth.
Characterization

Shelley calls the book her "hideous progeny" and sends it out into the world, as Victor does his creature; but unlike Victor she wishes it to "prosper." The author models the care the character fails to give. The words “Introduction” (Introduction, paragraph 15) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: Shelley calls the book her "hideous progeny" and sends it out into the world, as Victor does his creature; but unlike Victor she wishes it to "prosper." The author models the care the character fails to give. By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make.

The first sentence already contains a warning (his sister's "evil forebodings"). Strong evidence for foreshadowing. This develops ambition and knowledge: Walton dreams of "a part of the world never before visited." The novel begins with a second Victor before we meet the first. His dream of a land "never before visited" and his heart that glows with enthusiasm use the same fevered vocabulary Victor will use about creating life, which invites readers to compare the two men.

The "determined heart and resolved will of man" sounds heroic but is the attitude the novel interrogates. This develops ambition and knowledge: the "determined heart and resolved will of man" sounds heroic but is the attitude the novel interrogates. Asking "What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?" assumes nothing can; the rest of the book, beginning with the ice that traps his ship, shows that something always does.

Victor recognizes himself in Walton and warns him; the story becomes a cautionary tale told for a listener's benefit. This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor recognizes himself in Walton and warns him; the story becomes a cautionary tale told for a listener's benefit. By calling Walton's desire an "intoxicating draught" and hoping it will not be "a serpent to sting you," Victor links the pursuit of knowledge to addiction and to the biblical Fall, so everything he tells next is offered as a lesson.

"Divine" means to discover by intuition and also suggests godlike power. This develops ambition and knowledge: the desire to learn "the secrets of heaven and earth" begins as wonder and becomes obsession. Calling natural philosophy "the genius that has regulated my fate" makes science an outside force, and he blames his father's careless "sad trash" for not stopping him; readers can see a man explaining away his own will.

answerKey.answer: decipher
"Unhallowed" means unholy, and "thing" refuses the creation a name. Students can use this to argue that the novel judges the act of creation as a transgression from its first image.
Shelley's theory of creativity: you build from existing materials, as Victor builds from old bones. Good evidence for a claim about the novel's self-awareness.

Political education; links to Godwin. The words “I heard of the division of property, of immense wealth and squalid poverty; of rank, descent, and noble blood” (Chapter XIII, paragraph 16) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
Language, knowledge and sorrow

His education; each book shapes him. The words “Paradise Lost, a volume of Plutarch’s Lives, and the Sorrows of Werther” (Chapter XV, paragraph 3) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.

Isolation through allusion. The words “Like Adam, I was apparently united by no link to any other being in existence” (Chapter XV, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself.
Point of view

Places the book in real time and place; compare with the 1831 Introduction's fuller account. The words “I passed the summer of 1816 in the environs of Geneva” (Preface, paragraph 4) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: The Preface claims the story shows "the amiableness of domestic affection"; keep this phrase on the board. The novel will test it: domestic love is shown, then destroyed.

Religious, heightened language for exploration; compare later with Victor's rapture. The words “I feel my heart glow with an enthusiasm which elevates me to heaven” (Letter I, paragraph 3) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: Walton dreams of "a part of the world never before visited." The novel begins with a second Victor before we meet the first.
Tone / mood

The serpent alludes to Eden: knowledge as temptation and fall. Strong for a theme claim. The words “You seek for knowledge and wisdom, as I once did; and I ardently hope that the gratification of your wishes may not be a serpent to sting…” (Letter IV, paragraph 32) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor recognizes himself in Walton and warns him; the story becomes a cautionary tale told for a listener's benefit.

Possessive language; evidence for a claim about Victor's self-centeredness. The words “looked upon Elizabeth as mine—mine to protect, love, and cherish” (Chapter I, paragraph 11) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: The parents' "deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life" is the novel's standard of parental duty.

Calling natural philosophy "the genius that has regulated my fate" makes science an outside force, and he blames his father's careless "sad trash" for not stopping him; readers can see a man explaining away his own will. The words “Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate” (Chapter II, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: the desire to learn "the secrets of heaven and earth" begins as wonder and becomes obsession.
Creation and responsibility
Plot

He decides that "nothing in human shape could have destroyed that fair child," so he is certain who did it, yet he lets Justine be accused rather than reveal his secret. The words “Nothing in human shape could have destroyed that fair child” (Chapter VII, paragraph 29) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: the first death caused (indirectly) by Victor's creation.

Biblical image of hell (Isaiah, Mark): remorse as eternal torment. The words “the never-dying worm alive in my bosom” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 29) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: guilt without action: Victor feels remorse but does not act.

He claims "the tortures of the accused did not equal mine," even though she is the one executed, so his remorse becomes another form of self-focus rather than action. The words “The tortures of the accused did not equal mine” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 11) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: guilt without action: Victor feels remorse but does not act.

Claims a relationship and a duty. The words “Remember, that I am thy creature” (Chapter X, paragraph 12) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops nature and nurture: "I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend": the novel's clearest statement of the argument.

He remembers "considerable difficulty" in understanding his first sensations, a newborn's helplessness, and the villagers' response to his approach is that "some fled, some attacked me," so hostility comes from them. The words “It is with considerable difficulty that I remember the original era of my being” (Chapter XI, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops nature and nurture: he begins innocent; humans attack him on sight.

When he realizes that stealing "inflicted pain on the cottagers," he "abstained," choosing others' welfare over his own hunger without being taught. The words “when I found that in doing this I inflicted pain on the cottagers, I abstained” (Chapter XII, paragraph 6) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops nature and nurture: he learns virtue by watching virtue.

A question of identity. The words “And what was I” (Chapter XIII, paragraph 17) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: "Of what a strange nature is knowledge!": knowledge as a burden.

The creature curses his own birth, echoing Job. The words “Hateful day when I received life” (Chapter XV, paragraph 8) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops nature and nurture: rejection is based on sight; the blind man alone judges him by his words.
Chapter XVII

The wish to belong. The words “I shall feel the affections of a sensitive being, and become linked to the chain of existence and events, from which I am now excluded” (Chapter XVII, paragraph 14) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: the plea for a companion is the novel's most direct statement of the need for love.

The master has become the slave; a reversal the creature will state aloud in Chapter XX. The words “I was the slave of my creature” (Chapter XVIII, paragraph 13) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: Victor feels "an insurmountable barrier" between himself and others.
Chapter XIX

The creature reverses the master-slave relationship. The words “Slave, I before reasoned with you, but you have proved yourself unworthy of my condescension” (Chapter XX, paragraph 11) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: is destroying the female responsible or another betrayal?.
Foreshadowing
Creation and responsibility
Chapter XXI

He says "a fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness," the same hopeless isolation the creature described, and like the creature he turns to vengeance. The words “A fiend had snatched from me every hope of future happiness” (Chapter XXIII, paragraph 14) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: Victor becomes the pursuer.
Characterization

Shelley presents herself as a parent of the book. Use this to connect author and character: both make something "hideous," but only one blesses it. The words “And now, once again, I bid my hideous progeny go forth and prosper” (Introduction, paragraph 15) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: Shelley calls the book her "hideous progeny" and sends it out into the world, as Victor does his creature; but unlike Victor she wishes it to "prosper." The author models the care the character fails to give. By calling the book her "hideous progeny" she uses the language of parenthood; wishing it to "prosper" is exactly the blessing the creature never receives, so the frame sets up the novel's test of what makers owe what they make.

A careful double negative: not "possible," only "not impossible." Evidence that the book presents itself as grounded in real science. The words “The event on which this fiction is founded, has been supposed, by Dr. Darwin, and some of the physiological writers of Germany, as not of…” (Preface, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: The Preface claims the story shows "the amiableness of domestic affection"; keep this phrase on the board. The novel will test it: domestic love is shown, then destroyed. By citing Dr. Darwin and German physiologists it claims the event is "not of impossible occurrence," and by naming domestic affection and virtue as its aims it answers the charge that a horror story is immoral.

The first sentence already contains a warning (his sister's "evil forebodings"). Strong evidence for foreshadowing. The words “You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil…” (Letter I, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: Walton dreams of "a part of the world never before visited." The novel begins with a second Victor before we meet the first. His dream of a land "never before visited" and his heart that glows with enthusiasm use the same fevered vocabulary Victor will use about creating life, which invites readers to compare the two men.

The creature will ask for exactly this. Evidence that the need for companionship is universal in the novel. The words “I desire the company of a man who could sympathise with me; whose eyes would reply to mine” (Letter II, paragraph 2) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: the desire for a sympathetic friend is the thread connecting Walton, Victor and the creature. His wish for someone whose "eyes would reply to mine" names the sympathy every major character lacks, so the novel ties ambition to isolation from its first pages.

A rhetorical question the novel answers: nature, death and conscience can. The words “What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man” (Letter III, paragraph 4) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: the "determined heart and resolved will of man" sounds heroic but is the attitude the novel interrogates. Asking "What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?" assumes nothing can; the rest of the book, beginning with the ice that traps his ship, shows that something always does.

Opens with pride in lineage and status. The words “I am by birth a Genevese; and my family is one of the most distinguished of that republic” (Chapter I, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: The parents' "deep consciousness of what they owed towards the being to which they had given life" is the novel's standard of parental duty. He describes himself as the center of his parents' devotion and treats Elizabeth as his "present," showing that he received care as his due; when he refuses any care to his own creation, the contrast exposes his failure.

Waldman's contrast between old and modern science. The words “promised impossibilities, and performed nothing” (Chapter III, paragraph 16) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: Waldman says modern scientists "penetrate into the recesses of nature"; Victor answers with a vow to go further. Right after his mother's death he hears Waldman praise modern science and vows "more, far more, will I achieve," showing ambition rushing to fill the space left by loss.

Desire for glory, not care; evidence of selfish motives. The words “A new species would bless me as its creator and source” (Chapter IV, paragraph 8) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops ambition and knowledge: Victor fantasizes that "a new species would bless me as its creator," revealing the wish to be worshipped. He imagines a new species that "would bless me as its creator," which centers his own glory; nothing in his plans considers what the being will need.

The turn from ambition to revulsion in one sentence. The words “the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart” (Chapter V, paragraph 3) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops creation and responsibility: the moment of birth is the moment of abandonment. The creature's "hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me," a gesture of need, and Victor simply "escaped"; the word "seemingly" shows he does not know what it wants and does not stay to find out.

Victor names his work "selfish": a rare admission and strong evidence. The words “A selfish pursuit had cramped and narrowed me, until your gentleness and affection warmed and opened my senses” (Chapter VI, paragraph 21) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops isolation and companionship: Clerval shows what companionship gives: Victor says a selfish pursuit had "cramped and narrowed" him. Victor credits Clerval's "gentleness and affection" for curing what a "selfish pursuit" had done, so he knows what care is; he has simply not given it to his creation.

Elizabeth sees what Victor hides; his guilt shows on his face. The words “There is an expression of despair, and sometimes of revenge, in your countenance, that makes me tremble” (Chapter IX, paragraph 9) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the sublime: nature offers temporary relief from guilt. He describes "the dead calmness of inaction and certainty" as the most painful state of mind, and his remorse becomes "a hell of intense tortures"; suffering replaces confession, so guilt leads nowhere.

It clings to the mind, when it has once seized on it, like a lichen on the rock” (Chapter XIII, paragraph 19) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. He fears "the vengeance of the disappointed fiend" but cannot overcome his "repugnance to the task," and so he drifts; by his own admission he becomes "the slave of my creature.".

He fears "the vengeance of the disappointed fiend" but cannot overcome his "repugnance to the task," and so he drifts; by his own admission he becomes "the slave of my creature.".

essayAssignments.title: Essay: The costs of unchecked ambition

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Frankenstein teaches about the costs of unchecked ambition. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition across Frankenstein. Trace the idea through at least three chapters and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Frankenstein (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of the costs of unchecked ambition. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Mary Shelley's choices in Frankenstein (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of the costs of unchecked ambition, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about the costs of unchecked ambition in Frankenstein, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on nature versus nurture in Frankenstein that reads the novel against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on nature versus nurture in Frankenstein. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about nature versus nurture in Frankenstein, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on nature versus nurture in Frankenstein, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

essayAssignments.title: Essay: The sublime power of nature

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Frankenstein teaches about the sublime power of nature. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how Mary Shelley develops the sublime power of nature in Frankenstein. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Mary Shelley develops the sublime power of nature across Frankenstein. Trace the idea through at least three chapters and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Frankenstein (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of the sublime power of nature. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of the sublime power of nature in Frankenstein. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how Mary Shelley's choices in Frankenstein (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of the sublime power of nature, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

prompts.text: Analyze how Mary Shelley develops the costs of unchecked ambition across Frankenstein. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Frankenstein and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to creation and responsibility.
Analyze a central character's choices in Frankenstein. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether Frankenstein finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of isolation and the need for companionship. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the chapter and paragraph (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

criticalVoices.quote: Frightful must it be; for supremely frightful would be the effect of any human endeavour to mock the stupendous mechanism of the Creator of the world.
criticalVoices.speaker: Mary Shelley, author (Introduction to the revised edition, 1831)
criticalVoices.source: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus (London: Colburn and Bentley, 1831), Author's Introduction, Introduction, the waking-dream paragraph
criticalVoices.useNote: Thesis test: does the 1831 author frame ambition as blasphemy, and does the 1818 novel itself make that judgment? Students weigh the author's later frame against Walton's last letters (outside source for HS Senior and up; this introduction is not in the 1818 text).
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Final paper Prompt 1: trace the costs of unchecked ambition and argue what the ending suggests.

criticalVoices.quote: Nor are the crimes and malevolence of the single Being, though indeed withering and tremendous, the offspring of any unaccountable propensity to evil, but flow irresistibly from certain causes fully adequate to their production. They are the children, as it were, of Necessity and Human Nature.
criticalVoices.speaker: Percy Bysshe Shelley, poet
criticalVoices.source: "On 'Frankenstein'" (written c.1817; pub. The Athenaeum, 10 Nov 1832), in The Prose Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley (1880), paragraph 2
criticalVoices.useNote: Counter-argument starter: use Shelley as the "society made him" reading, then answer the strongest objection (the murders of William and Elizabeth) from the Creature's own words in the last chapter.
